entries.title: What’s the Best Pet DNA Test? We Tested the Most Popular Ones
entries.summary: I sent my cats’ saliva to the lab to get health and genetic insights sent to my inbox—with very different results.
entries.content:
An at-home cat or dog DNA test kit promises to give pet owners clarity on a heap of important health data, like breed ancestry, blood type, and health risks. To access this info, owners just swab the inside of their pet’s mouth, seal the sample in a prepaid-postage envelope, and wait (for up to five weeks) for results to be sent to their inbox. Each company has a testing lab, and the results live in your online account, where they can be downloaded and even shared with your vet.

But because of several factors, such as sample size and comparison, these tests often give dramatically different results for things like genetic ancestry and breed traits (more on that below).

I tested several at-home DNA test kits, including two of the most popular kits—Basepaws ($104) and Wisdom Panel ($97)—on my two adult cats and talked to several animal experts to get insights into these tests—and whether they are worth your money, given the large disparity in results. Think of this as the WIRED guide to the increasingly popular at-home pet DNA test.

Table of Contents

Be sure to check out our related guides, like the Best Automatic Cat Feeders, Best Automatic Litter Boxes, Best Automatic Cat Fountains, and Best Dog Accessories.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Easiest Interface

Breed Health Test Trait Test Blood Type/Transfusion Risk Oral Health Report Family Tree
Wisdom Panel (Cat) Screens for 70+ breeds and populations Tests for 45+ genetic health conditions Test for 25+ physical traits Yes No Yes

In my research, I've found that people widely consider Wisdom Panel the most trusted at-home pet DNA test kit (along with dog-only Embark, which former WIRED reviewer Julia Forbes tested below).

Wisdom Panel offers several kits for dogs (listed below) but only one test for cats. It can identify more than 70 breeds, includes 45 health tests, determines blood type, and screens for more than 25 traits. It even provides a genetic consult for “at-risk” health findings and shows what the pet's family tree might look like based on DNA results. I especially liked that it tests for the most common conditions seen in cats or dogs with a similar breed makeup to your pet (based on the DNA sample), including important markers like drug sensitivity, immune deficiency, and bleeding disorders. It also identified the cat’s blood type (both of my cats were A) and transfusion risk (both were moderate).

The results arrived live online in my Wisdom Panel account within three weeks of mailing them. I really appreciated the interface, which was organized into clickable tabs that made the information easier to access and navigate. Plus, based on appearance alone, my cat Clover's DNA results seemed most accurate with this test (below). I also tested my run-of-the-mill gray tabby cat, Basil, but on all tests—including Wisdom Panel—he was almost entirely labeled as an “American domestic cat” and “polycat/domestic shorthair." That's basically the mutt final boss, a result of many generations of mixed breeding among different cat types, where ancestry and origin are almost impossible to determine.

Clover’s Wisdom Panel Results
American domestic cat: 51 percent
Highlander: 13 percent
Norwegian Forest Cat: 13 percent
Siamese and Oriental: 13 percent
LaPerm: 10 percent

Most In-Depth Results

Breed Health Test Trait Test Blood Type/Transfusion Risk Oral Health Report Family Tree
Basepaws (Cat) Tests against 21 breeds Tests for 64 genetic health markers Tests for 50 genetic trait markers Yes Yes No

WIRED reviewed Basepaws over half a decade ago, and a lot has changed since then. Basepaws offers a single breed and health test for cats that identifies up to 21 breeds, 64 genetic health markers, 50 genetic trait markers, blood type, and oral health. The wait time for results is five weeks, and when I first sent my cat Basil's test in, they couldn't extract enough DNA, so I had to send another sample and wait another five weeks. Rather than an easily digestible interactive screen with information like Wisdom Panel, Basepaws gives you essentially a mini book PDF to scroll through to find information. It feels more in-depth than Wisdom Panel, but it is also harder to disseminate the large pile of information.

Basepaws tests genes for markers associated with disorders in musculoskeletal and connective tissue; eyes; metabolic, autoimmune, and endocrine systems; blood; and more. Both of my cats, Clover and Basil, were cleared of any genes that would mark them as potential carriers of genetic diseases. It also identified blood type and transfusion risk, which were A and moderate (the same results I got with Wisdom Panel’s test).

Basepaws tests for oral health by comparing against an oral microbiome database. In this regard, Basepaws wins out. Dental health is a major concern for me, and I love that Basepaws screens for it and provides an oral health report (I have since started brushing my cats' teeth). My cat Basil was at high risk for all dental markers like halitosis, tooth resorption, and periodontal disease. Basepaws developed a health plan for him: “Adopt a daily oral health care routine, consider supplementing Basil’s routine with products accepted by the Veterinary Oral Health Council, and schedule an appointment with your veterinarian in the next month.” Although I was alarmed by the results, I appreciated that Basepaws provided recommended next steps so I could develop a plan of action for care. And it’s important to remember that these results don’t necessarily mean a pet is guaranteed to develop the disease.

"These can be a helpful flag for your veterinarian to keep an eye on [...] but do not necessarily mean aggressive testing is needed at that moment,” says Jamie Richardson, head of veterinary medicine at Small Door Veterinary. “DNA tests are tools to support—not replace—veterinary care.”

Some of the other Basepaws results, particularly the genetic and physical markers, seem off. Like Wisdom Panel, white calico Clover was marked as “likely” to be black in color, and none of the ancestral DNA breeds matched across tests for Clover.

Clover’s Basepaws Results
Polycat (domestic shorthair): 20.61 percent
Broadly Western: 16.91 percent
American Shorthair: 14.45 percent
Maine coon: 12.27 percent
Ragdoll: 11.8 percent
Persian: 6.99 percent
Siberian: 6.2 percent
Abyssinian: 5.62 percent
Burmese: 3.07 percent
Savannah: 2.08 percent

Another Cat DNA Test Kit I Tested

Breed Health Test Trait Test Blood Type/Transfusion Risk Oral Health Report Family Tree
Koko Genetics Yes; tests against an unspecified number Tests for 55 genetic health markers Tests for 40 traits No No Yes

Koko Genetics was a new name to me, but it offers a similar service to the two major brands above, with tests for both cats and dogs in “starter” basic and “advanced” kits. I tested the latter, which provides additional health insights by screening for genetic disorders or abnormalities. The process is exactly the same as with the other kits, where you swab your cat's mouth, register your kit online, and mail the results. The Koko Genetics interface wouldn't allow me to register two kits with different cats under the same login/username, so I had to create two separate accounts with two different emails, which was a slight pain. The results also took surprisingly long—it took over five weeks from mailing to being acknowledged as received, and an additional five weeks to get results.

This interface was the least user-friendly of all I tested, and many of the default options were in Spanish with no English options. The site where you access results is a little bare-bones, with additional information available if you click the tab. I found that much of the health trait info was scientific jargon, and I had to do further research to understand it. Clover was flagged as having a copy of the Acute Intermittent Porphyria (Variant 3) gene mutation, which can cause discolored teeth and urine and may lead to other health problems. Luckily, Clover has just one copy of the mutation and will not develop the disease, but she can transmit the mutation to her offspring. (She's spayed, so that is not a potential issue.) Wisdom Panel also tests for this, and she was not flagged as carrying it in that test.

Both cats were negative for all physical traits except black coat (which neither has), and I didn't find the info really helpful or interesting. There's also a family tree option, like Wisdom Panel's, where you can see what the previous generations' breed or coloring might've been.

Clover’s Koko Genetics Results
Domestic cat: 59.5 percent
Sphynx: 8.8 percent
Turkish Van: 6.6 percent
Maine Coon: 6.3 percent
LaPerm: 5.7 percent
Munchkin cat: 4.6 percent
Norwegian Forest Cat: 4.4 percent
Chartreux: 4.1 percent

Best Dog DNA Test Kit

Breed Health Test Trait Test Blood Type/Transfusion Risk Oral Health Report Family Tree
Embark Dog Tests against over 400 breeds No No; results for likely personality traits rather than physical No No Yes

One of my family’s favorite pastimes is placing low-stakes bets on the breeds that make up our beloved rescue dogs. Usually we’re wildly off with our estimates. For my dog Randy, all we knew was that he was a Chihuahua mix. The Embark DNA kit is the dog equivalent of Ancestry DNA for humans, given how detailed it is. The test kit uses a saliva sample, and you ship it off for processing. Within three weeks, we found out Randy had quite the cocker spaniel lineage, with show-dog cousins across the country (Princess Elysia of Eagle’s Wings’ parents, if you’re reading this, hello!).

The Embark app gives detailed breakdowns of behavioral, health, and longevity insights for the breeds that make up your pup. His personality analysis shows he’s closely aligned with his cocker spaniel roots, always on the lookout (check), sometimes high-energy (check), and rarely independent (spot on). —Julia Forbes

The kits below are also specifically for dogs from Basepaws and Wisdom Panel, two companies I've tested on my cats.

How Does a DNA Test Kit Work?

Pet DNA tests rely on pet owners collecting cells via a cheek swab, then placing the sample in a sealed stabilizing or preserving fluid for transit. You’ll mail the sample back to the lab in the prepaid envelope. It usually takes about five weeks to get results. (The first time I sent my cat Basil’s Basepaws sample, the company emailed that the results were inconclusive, and I had to wait for another kit to be sent, re-swab him, and wait another five weeks for results.)

At the lab, the sample is analyzed against the company’s breed and genetic health database. They use single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays—the standard technology for identifying breed ancestry—as well as data on inherited traits and the risk of common diseases. Essentially, different breeds have distinct patterns of SNPs in their genomes, which serve as genetic markers. These tests analyze the pet’s DNA sample for specific SNPs and then compare them to the company’s existing database to estimate the animal’s breed composition. This not only tells you about breed composition, but can also identify the specific DNA sequences that are markers for potential health risks, such as predispositions to diseases or hereditary cancers.

Don’t take the health or DNA test results as absolute truth, however. “This can lead to a false sense of security or false alarms," says veterinarian Amanda Chambers. Forward your results to your veterinarian and always follow up by scheduling a visit to the vet if your pet is marked as a carrier for any genetic disease.

What the Results Can—and Can’t—Tell You

After chatting with Richardson, I’ve found that these are the major areas of limitation with at-home DNA test kits:

  • Results depend on the size/diversity of the genetic database
  • Most kits test known markers only—not full genomes
  • Feline data is less developed
  • Misinterpretation of results can lead to unnecessary concern

Wisdom Panel claims its cat breed results are over 98 percent accurate and its dog tests are over 99 percent accurate. However, there's a huge disparity between the three kits I tested on my cats, particularly in breed ancestry. One problem with the vast disparity in results is that the three companies use different sample sizes and metrics to identify breeds.

But the biggest issue for cat owners taking these at-home DNA tests is that you can’t really identify most cats' breeds the way you can with dogs. Unless your cat is a purebred, about 95 percent of cats don’t belong to a recognized breed. Cats' genetic backgrounds are muddied—they're just similar mixes with different physical characteristics, so the tests only show the breed(s) they share the most markers with. Basically, these tests for cats aren’t able to reliably tell us about breed composition, just similarity to other breeds’ traits in the company’s data pool.

From my research, it seems the breed identification part of these tests is more accurate for dogs, as dog DNA is so much more diversified. Breeds have been clearly defined after centuries of diversification, and dog DNA mutates quickly, with genes changing after just a few generations. Cats are not much different from their Egyptian ancestors.

Interestingly, in a 2023 CBS report, the news organization sent dog and human DNA to different at-home test companies and received varying results, with the dog's DNA ranging from 65 to only 29 percent German Shepherd. The human DNA results were attributed to a bulldog, border collie, and cane corso mix.

In summation, unfortunately, there isn't a single catchall way to determine a pet's genetic makeup or ancestry. Humans like categories, and breeds are essentially human constructs based on how a dog or cat looks. The genetic part of the test is fun, but take it with a grain of salt—especially with cats.

A Note on At-Home Allergy Testing Kits

I recently tested both of my cats for allergies and intolerances using a similar at-home test kit, the 5Strands Pet Food & Environmental Intolerance Test, for $100. For this, you only need to send a fur sample in the mail to a lab; results were sent to my inbox within seven days. The report showed that both of my cats had strong intolerances to common ingredients in their diet, such as various types of fish and chicken meal. This sent me into a panic about my cats' health and (dis)comfort.

After further research, I learned that hair/fur samples are not an accurate way to measure allergies and intolerances. Studies show that kits claiming to provide these results perform no better than chance and often produce inconsistent or false results.

“There's no scientific evidence to support allergy testing through hair, fur, or saliva,” says Richardson. “Veterinarian-supervised elimination diets to test for food allergy and intradermal skin testing or blood tests to test for environmental allergies remain the gold standard.”

So, save your money and consult a vet instead if you suspect your pet is suffering from allergies or intolerances.

Meet the Experts

  • Amanda Chambers is a full-time small animal general practitioner based in Kansas City, Missouri.
  • Jamie Richardson is head of veterinary medicine at Small Door Veterinary.

entries.title: You Don’t Need to Pay for Distraction-Blocking Software
entries.summary: These free iOS and Android apps create the physical friction you need to put down your phone.
entries.content:
Wish you looked at your phone less? Then you’ve probably heard of Brick, a $59 device that claims to help you block distractions. You tap your phone against the Brick when you want to avoid distractions—the bundled software stops you from opening whichever apps you’ve decided you need to stop doomscrolling.

The idea is to add a physical barrier between you and apps like Instagram—if you want to scroll, you need to physically get up, find the Brick, and tap it. It’s a good idea, and implemented in a way that makes it easy to get started. But what if you don’t want to buy a chunk of plastic?

Good news: the Brick is basically just an NFC chip, not that different from the one in your credit card or passport. You can buy a blank NFC chip for a dollar. Even better, free applications can use these chips to block distractions, exactly like the Brick. Or, if you prefer, these apps also support QR codes, meaning all you need is a printer. Here are two free distraction-blocking apps—complete with physical barriers—for iPhone or Android.

Best for iPhones: Foqos

The oddly named Foqos is a free, open source app for iOS by Canadian developer Ali Waseem. Many open source apps lack polish, but not this one—it’s easy to configure the necessary permissions, set up a profile, and start blocking distractions.

While creating a new profile, you first choose which physical object you want to use to start and stop your blocking sessions. The two most popular options are NFC tags (there’s a handy link to buy some in the app) or a QR code. But you can also block using a daily schedule, if you prefer, or by scanning any barcode. The barcode option is nice because you don’t need to buy or print anything—scan the code on your favorite book, beverage, or anything else you keep around the house.

Foqos can block you from managing apps while a profile is running. This means you can’t just delete Foqos to get around a block you set up, which is exactly what someone fighting against their own urges needs. You can allow a limited number of breaks, if you want.

I’ve been using this to break my Reddit habit and can report that it works. I keep a printed QR code inside a cabinet, far from the couch where I tend to scroll. It creates just enough friction that I can finish reading a book instead. The application has an excellent privacy policy—no data leaves your device.

Best for Android: Switchly

Foqos is sadly iOS-exclusive, and I couldn’t find an Android equivalent that’s quite as polished. But Switchly, by Vienna-based developer Saltyy, stands out as one of the more feature-complete apps I tested. You will need to spend some time fiddling to get it set up, granted, but once you do, you’ll find it every bit as flexible as Foqos.

To get started, open the app, which you can install from Google Play. A wizard will guide you through the relevant permissions, then talk you through setting up your first profile. You will need to read everything carefully, because it’s a little bit tough to navigate the first time. You can block apps and URLs. You can use an NFC chip or a QR code to trigger locking and unlocking. You can also block based on a schedule; Premium users can trigger when connected to a particular Wi-Fi network, or when a certain Bluetooth device is nearby.

If you’d rather not block Instagram entirely, but never want to see a Reel again, good news: there’s support for blocking particular features inside certain apps. The feature is labeled as experimental, but worked well in my testing.

There’s a lot of flexibility, but Android’s open nature means how well it works depends in part on your phone model. The developer acknowledges this. Also, you don’t need the Premium version—the free tier offers plenty of features for most people.

Another application Android users should check out is Lock. This app is more polished than Switchly, but only supports NFC chips. Give it a try if Switchly doesn’t quite work the way you like.

Distractions don’t just live on your phone. We’ve written about how to block websites on your computer, with multiple free options. But let’s face it: the phone is the ultimate distraction machine. Learn to control your impulses there.

entries.title: The Data Center Backlash Should Also Be a Climate Reckoning. It Isn’t Yet
entries.summary: Climate groups are latching onto the data center opposition movement, but it remains to be seen if they can get people to care about the facilities’ impact on the atmosphere.
entries.content:
Welcome to the latest edition of Power Play! From now until the midterms, senior writer Molly Taft will be sharing their thoughts every Sunday on this political season’s hottest issue: data centers. We welcome reader comments, and will be answering questions from the comments section in future editions.

The post-lunchtime Climate Week panel featuring tech executives working on AI and data centers was only about a minute into the discussion when a man stood up a few rows over from me in the audience and started yelling.

“The idea that we can keep running on fracked gas is a lie!” he exclaimed as security tackled him.

The panel tried to get back to business after the protester was removed—only to be interrupted again when another person stood up. That’s how things proceeded for the next 10 minutes as protesters with the group Extinction Rebellion NYC staggered interruptions, yelling about various harms of AI over the speakers onstage, who tried valiantly to continue their conversation.

For nearly a decade, Extinction Rebellion groups have used public protest to draw attention to the climate emergency, staging disruptions at corporate-friendly events like this one at Climate Week. Usually, these types of interruptions draw polite silences or subtle eyerolls from panelists waiting for them to stop.

But this experience seemed particularly frustrating to these panelists. Cully Cavness, the cofounder and president of data center infrastructure company Crusoe, confessed to the session’s moderator that he was still thinking about the interruption several minutes after security had taken the last protester out.

I get why they were on edge. The protest at the panel was a microcosm of the tough couple of months for data center defenders, with public opinion at rock-bottom levels and moratoriums popping up in red and blue states. It’s understandable why tech folks would be tense.

Cavness, at one point, said that he assumed most of the protesters probably didn’t even live near a data center and didn’t understand the benefits they could bring to the local tax base. Emerald AI’s Varun Sivaram forged ahead talking about how data centers could become “good citizens,” to work on the grid to lower bills and bring more clean energy online.

“Careful what you wish for,” Sivaram cautioned the now-absent protesters near the end of the session, warning that depriving communities of data centers could deprive them of good actors to help transform the grid.

Lots of folks might take the opportunity, as the protesters did, to yell at a data center executive if given the chance. But unlike the Extinction Rebellion NYC members, climate change almost certainly wouldn’t be the first thing on their minds. Data centers were a hot topic at Climate Week, but it’s also a self-selecting event where people care about one particular issue.

Local concerns—the kind Sivaram and Cavness seemed to be responding to—have dominated the larger national conversation around data center dissent. Poll after poll show that climate is one of the last data center-related environmental concerns on the list for many voters behind water, energy use (and its impact on bills), and local air and noise pollution. Even some climate folks—notably investors—see the state of the atmosphere as a backseat issue. “Climate Week could basically be ‘AI and data center week,” cofounder and managing partner at VoLo Earth told the Wall Street Journal. “It’s all about energy, and most of us as climate investors, myself included, are focused on the energy system.”

During Climate Week, I also caught up with William Lawrence, who is currently locked in a tight race for Michigan’s 7th congressional district. Lawrence knows the climate crisis well—he’s one of the original founders of the Sunrise Movement climate activist group. He’s also made data center opposition, as well as opposition to AI, a cornerstone of his pitch to voters, which helped him win a tough Democratic primary.

Lawrence says there are at least three hyperscalers building projects in his district, and he just released a wide-ranging platform to stop AI development. The platform says that data centers “threaten our air, water and quality of life,” but makes no mention of climate change. When I ask him about the omission, he says that there are Michiganders coming to him with climate concerns about data centers, although water concerns and energy bills tend to rank higher. He says that in general, there’s a strong “environmental consciousness” animating the data center movementt—which may include climate, but isn’t always expressed exclusively in terms of worries about emissions.

“We have a small amount of billionaires and political insiders who have made it impossible to feel confident about the future,” he says. “They’ve destabilized our ecological system. They’ve destabilized the political order.”

Sivaram’s point that the massive influx of electricity demand from data centers could help to transform our electricity sector for the better is true. Unfortunately, that’s not what’s happening on the ground, where data centers are facilitating a massive fossil fuel buildout that’s happening faster than expected.

A day before the panel, at a different briefing, I watched BloombergNEF analysts talk about the group’s projections of a massive new influx of demand for fossil fuel power over the coming years, driven primarily by data centers. Data centers, according to BNEF’s analysis, will likely comprise more than 5 percent of global electricity demand by 2035, tripling their needs now. The majority of that demand will be met by new and existing natural gas plants, and could raise the power sector’s emissions by 6 percent in less than 10 years.

That doesn’t even account for gas power plants being built off the grid to service data centers. A separate BNEF analysis of 99 proposed on-site gas power plants found that they could increase US power sector emissions by 20 to 33 percent if they’re all built, posing a major climate threat. Declines in emissions from coal plant retirements will be more than offset by new gas emissions, and more coal plants are staying online thanks to the new demand.

Even if data centers pull off the PR turnaround of the century and ease concerns about water use and energy bills, the fossil fuel buildout still looms as one of the biggest consequences of their buildout. Extinction Rebellion may, at the end of the day, be right: all those added emissions mean that even those of us who aren’t living near data centers will end up feeling their impacts.

What We’re Writing

If the data center gas buildout keeps raring ahead, the climate is going to need all the help it can get. This week, I covered the launch of a new startup that aims to use supercritical CO2 technology to make dirty data center gas turbines more efficient. It’s been studied for decades as a potential energy solution, but it’s yet to be successfully commercialized. The founders hope that deep-pocketed data center operators that are also hungry for power will bet on the tech to meet some of their energy needs and help bring down costs. Eventually, they want to expand the use of the technology to supercharge clean energy sources, like nuclear.

What We’re Reading

  • Google will launch an experimental satellite next week outfitted with computer chips to test how data centers may perform in space. The company says the satellite will stay in orbit for a year; its equipment will answer "simple queries," the New York Times reports.
  • Oracle has sent a force majeure notice, which could allow it to delay payments to the developer of its data center project in New Mexico, which has been plagued by multiple local environmental challenges and permitting issues. Bloomberg broke the story.
  • Should Native American tribes support data center development? It's an issue splitting candidates and leaders all over the country; TIME has the story.

entries.title: Nicotine Is Mounting a Comeback in the Wellness Movement
entries.summary: Improving mood and increasing longevity are just some of the unfounded claims about this substance circling around the “natural” medicine corners of the internet.
entries.content:
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.

An ironic development emerging alongside the “Make America Healthy Again” movement is the portrayal of nicotine as a wellness and performance-enhancing product. Across social media, podcasts, natural medicine communities and tech startups, prominent wellness personalities and other influencers are portraying nicotine as a misunderstood compound whose potential benefits have been overshadowed by its negative association with cigarettes.

In these circles, nicotine is now being hailed as a natural product that can be used for everything from improving focus to protecting against cognitive decline. As a pulmonary physician-scientist who studies nicotine addiction and the health consequences of tobacco and nicotine products, I am concerned about these claims.

Some of this rebranding stems from the observation that nicotine is a naturally occurring plant compound found primarily in tobacco and in nightshade vegetables such as tomatoes, potatoes and eggplant in trace amounts. Proponents of nicotine use also draw on studies suggesting that nicotine can affect certain aspects of cognition and brain function. However, extending these findings to broad claims about productivity, brain health, longevity or wellness goes well beyond what has been shown in human studies.

The greatest health risks arise when tobacco is burned, which generates thousands of toxic substances, including carcinogens, carbon monoxide, and fine particulate matter. Repeated exposure to these combustion products can cause cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease, and numerous other smoking-related illnesses.

Nicotine’s comeback as a wellness product is more about non-smoking options, such as nicotine pouches, or some combine nicotine with other substances marketed as cognition enhancers, like caffeine and nootropics. While many smoking-related diseases result from the chemical products of combustion, nicotine itself has well-known negative effects on the brain and body.

Nicotine activates the sympathetic nervous system—the body’s “fight or flight” response—which increases heart rate and blood pressure and disrupts sleep. Repeatedly kick-starting this system can place additional strain on the heart. Exposure is also of particular concern during critical phases of development.

Not to mention the extremely well-known risk that nicotine is addictive. It activates reward pathways in the brain, acting on receptors for acetylcholine, a key neurotransmitter involved in attention, learning, and memory. Though it may temporarily increase alertness and attention, nicotine does not reproduce normal acetylcholine signaling. The effects last much longer and alter activity throughout the brain.

With repeated exposure, the brain adapts to nicotine’s presence. Receptors become less responsive, and so the brain compensates by increasing the number of nicotine receptors, contributing to dependence. Activation of these receptors also influences the release of other neurotransmitters, including dopamine, which plays an important role in reward and reinforcement.

A common claim within wellness communities is that nicotine is a cognitive enhancer that improves focus and productivity. While there are some studies indicating that nicotine may temporarily enhance attention, vigilance, reaction time, and some types of memory, the results are mixed.

If any benefit does exist, the research suggests that this may only be the case for people with mild cognitive impairment. For healthy individuals, it doesn’t appear to offer any boost and may even worsen cognitive operation among higher-performing people.

In addition, many of these studies include people already dependent on nicotine. When these regular users stop consuming nicotine, they’re likely to experience irritability, anxiety, restlessness, and impaired attention. Reintroducing nicotine often relieves these symptoms, making it difficult to determine whether any improvements reflect true cognitive enhancement or are simply the reversal of withdrawal symptoms.

Wellness influencers also promote nicotine as a tool for managing stress and improving mood. Nicotine does activate reward pathways in the brain, which can create a sense of pleasure and wellbeing—temporarily.

Long-term users of nicotine often find that the substance makes stress and anxiety harder to manage. Research consistently shows that people who quit smoking experience reductions in anxiety, depression, and stress, along with improvements in mood and overall quality of life over time. In fact, long-term discontinuation of nicotine use is associated with better mental health.

But the most ambitious claims emerging from the pro-nicotine wellness movement suggest that nicotine protects against Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s, and other forms age-related cognitive decline. Or further, that nicotine slows biological aging and promotes longevity.

There’s some kernels of research underneath these claims, such as laboratory studies showing that nicotine can affect cellular pathways related to oxidative stress and animal studies suggesting effects on inflammation and other mechanisms linked to aging and disease. However, such findings have not translated into anything that indicates nicotine promotes healthy aging, extends lifespan or prevents age-related disease in humans.

entries.title: Some Pancreatic Cells Are Just One Genetic Tweak Away From Treating Diabetes
entries.summary: By deactivating a gene, researchers were able to cause cells in the pancreatic ducts to produce insulin to regulate blood sugar.
entries.content:
A human pancreas typically contains about a billion beta cells, the primary producers of insulin. Among people with diabetes, these cells are either missing or dysfunctional, and thus scientists have been looking for ways to replenish their numbers as a possible long-term treatment or even cure for the condition. A team of researchers recently took a step closer to that reality, genetically altering another type of pancreatic cell to produce and release insulin in response to high blood sugar.

The researchers engineered ductal cells, which—as some previous studies had found—occasionally transform into beta cells all on their own. This is an unusual phenomenon among cells in adult bodies, which tend to be firmly fixed in their identities, and it hinted to the scientists that these ductal cells would be a good place to start.

Scientists previously had no clue what genes were driving this metamorphosis, said Jian Li, a postdoctoral researcher at Harvard Medical School who led the recent study in Science Translational Medicine. The researchers therefore took an approach called a genetic screen, which involves breaking little bits of DNA all across the genome to see which are important for a certain biological process. It’s a bit like individually removing pieces of a car engine without a schematic and seeing what breaks to learn which components are involved in delivering fuel or are essential for steering.

Through this process, the researchers found that taking out a gene called ALDH3B2 turned ductal cells into beta-like cells at a higher rate. Without the genetic alteration, fewer than 1 percent of ductal cells spontaneously took on a beta-cell-like state, but when ALDH3B2 was silenced, that proportion increased to about 8.5 percent.

Those initial experiments were performed on human cells in a dish, which the researchers then transplanted into mice with diabetes. Human insulin began circulating in the mice, and the animals’ glucose levels dropped to near-normal levels. These effects persisted for six weeks.

Science has previously explored some gene therapies for diabetes with the hopes of offering long-term relief. For example, a clinical trial launched earlier this year is taking the creative approach of equipping muscle cells with the genetic instructions to make insulin. Other emerging treatments aim to generate new insulin-producing cells in the laboratory and then transplant them into the patient.

This comes with a few risks, namely activation of the immune system. This new study points to another possibility: harnessing the cells that already exist in the pancreas and causing them to change function by turning off some of the genetic switches that maintain their identity.

That method also has its own hurdles, one of the most important of which is ensuring that only the target cells are edited. ALDH3B2 is used by many cells in the body, not just in the pancreas, so precision is important to prevent unforeseen complications.

There’s also a major lingering question: How is this gene involved in turning ductal cells into beta cells? “That's the part we need to verify first,” Li said. Then, “the next step is either gene therapy or to find specific small molecules to inhibit this gene to see if we can achieve a similar—or even better—effect.”

Even partial improvement could make a massive impact in the lives of the estimated 830 million people who have diabetes worldwide, including many who die each year due to related complications.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: Old-School Credit Card Scams Are Far From Dead
entries.summary: In an era of increasingly sophisticated AI-fueled scams, a retro threat may be lurking in your mailbox.
entries.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic! A weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

When every random text message feels like it’s a scam, and with AI supercharging digital fraud, old-time credit card skimmers and bogus letters that arrive in the mail may seem laughable as potential threats in 2026. But as we all suffer through a seemingly unending barrage of potential scams, these antiquated attacks are still costing victims around the world dearly.

The fake-new-credit-card-in-your-mailbox trick is particularly insidious. Portugal, France, and Germany have all had waves of physical credit card scams in recent years where criminals have mailed phony replacement cards or letters to potential victims. Included letters often claim a current card is set to expire soon, whether the victim actually has one that's about to expire or not. In order for the new (fake) card to be activated, the scam letter says, it should be registered using an included QR code or URL. Some sham cards even have real customer names printed on them, says Georg Hauer, an advisor for digital banks. “The card is almost like a token that creates the trust that is needed in order to fall for the actual trick,” he says.

If someone scans the QR code, they’re typically redirected to a fake banking website, where they’re asked to enter their details—potentially giving cybercriminals direct access to their real accounts. “This has been escalating for close to two years, and I believe that this type of scam might have proven to be successful enough to be rolled out in other countries,” Hauer says. “The cost of producing a personalized fake card has dropped in recent years thanks to AI just being able to copy a design based on an image, and the higher conversion rate per victim might justify the extra costs.”

Mail scams aren’t the only ’90s throwback on the docket. The US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Alabama indicted two Romanian nationals last week on charges related to alleged credit card skimming. Authorities say the pair specifically targeted government SNAP food assistance benefits distributed to recipients in most states on antiquated magnetic stripe-only debit cards, or Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards.

Fraud related to chip credit cards does exist as well, but this recent case serves as a reminder that classic skimmers targeting magnetic stripe credit cards are still deployed by scammers because there’s apparently still enough swiping going on to make it worth their while. The FBI says that EBT card skimming has risen in popularity among scammers since about 2021.

“Skimmer fraud is rampant with losses in the United States alone reaching over $1 billion each year,” US Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr. said in a press release about the recent indictment. (That billion dollars includes multiple types of credit card skimming, not just EBT targeting.) “It is a silent insidious theft that occurs by merely swiping a credit card at a point of sale.”

Gary Warner, the director of intelligence at the cybersecurity firm DarkTower points out that dozens of states continue to use mag-stripe only cards for benefits purposes. “The risk here is that if the mag stripe is compromised, a clone of the card can be created and access not only the current value, but future value as well,” he says.

More broadly, Warner tells us, there are still multiple risks related to making payments using the magnetic stripes on any cards—even if they also include more secure chips that have been issued over the last decade-plus. “Non-bank ATMs and smaller non-chain merchants may expose your chip-enabled card to mag stripe reading,” Warner says. “Mag-stripe skimmers are often installed in such a way that the chip read is forced to fail.”

While magnetic stripe cards have gradually been phased out in the US over many years, they’re still around. Mastercard, for example, said last month that it will stop issuing any cards with stripes in 2029, and its remaining batch will be completely out of circulation by 2033. In the meantime, financial fraud has become one of the largest overall crime types in the US and around the world. Many attacks are focused on social engineering, mass phishing message campaigns, and other fraud where money ends up being sent by victims in transactions that often look legitimate to banks and other financial institutions.

Hauer says criminals will always try to use methods that let them steal as much money as possible, even if that means sending physical letters in the mail. “The real idea behind some of these scams is to not essentially try to steal €2,000 from someone’s bank account, but rather actually empty a proper savings account, which holds much more money,” he says.

If you feel like you’re already dodging scams left and right, there are some (relatively) easy takeaways to protect yourself from these old time scams. Avoid swiping cards whenever possible. And when you do need to swipe—as is, of course, the case with many EBT cards—do your best to check whether the terminal you’re about to use looks unusual, altered, or broken in any way. If so, use a different terminal. And apply the same skepticism that you have about texts and calls to letters as well. It feels like the only organizations that send mail these days are marketers, healthcare providers, banks, and the IRS, but scammers are still lurking there, too.

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

entries.title: 12 Best White Elephant Gifts, Plus a Prank Box to Put Them In (2026)
entries.summary: Bring the gift everyone will want to win from this year’s holiday party, from a cute jacket for a beer can to magnets they’ll wish they could eat.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

You Can’t Escape the white elephant parties. My friend who hosts an annual white elephant is debating sending out an invite before October even begins, and my mother’s ornament-themed white elephant has split into two parties this year. On top of all your regular Christmas and holiday shopping, trying to pick a gift that won’t embarrass you at multiple gift exchanges feels like mental torture.

That’s because white elephant parties in particular present a unique challenge: Can you find a cool or funny white elephant gift within a set budget that a group of people—who are potentially strangers—will battle each other to take home? None of us want to be the person who brought the gift nobody wanted. Some folks bring joke gifts, some bring booze to be safe, and some gifts will feel like garbage to you but gems to others. Some of my favorite white elephant gifts include a coffee-pot-shaped mug, a fun Lego set, and sushi-shaped magnets. Here’s every white elephant gift I recommend bringing, ranging from quirky to cool to actually useful.

Looking for more gift ideas? Don’t miss our other awesome gift guides as the holiday season ramps up.

Updated October 2026: I’ve added new Lego sets, a cozy beverage set, and new e-reader case options, and checked to make sure everything else is still in stock.

Honorable Mentions

Nowadays Cannabis Infused Beverage, Starting at $40: Bringing a bottle of booze is a white elephant classic; my husband’s work team almost exclusively exchanges bottles of liquor as a safe bet for enthusiasm. I think you can do better, though, and bring a THC spirit instead. This spirit is light and a little fruity, sitting somewhere in between the flavor profile of a floral gin and a sweet sake. My friends and I tried it mixed into a pomegranate cocktail instead of tequila, which was fantastic, and we also loved it with seltzer as a THC twist on a gin and tonic. It’s delicious alone, too. I’d skip this for a work party or any group that might not be green-friendly, though.

Booze in general: This is always a safe pick! You could also bring a bottle of nonalcoholic wine if you wanted an option that everyone can have.

Something edible: As long as you’re in the loop on food allergies, of course. One of the best gifts I received at a Secret Santa was persimmon cookies, made in honor of my love for persimmon fruit. I think baking something delicious would be a fun option for a white elephant, too, especially if you’re someone who has sourdough starter in their kitchen or makes a mean banana bread (my version uses brown butter and Nutella, and it might be my gift of choice this year!)

What Not to Bring to a White Elephant

Here’s what was the least fought over at the white elephant parties I attended last year, or the most inappropriate ideas our team has heard of:

  • A basic, single candle. Nobody needs a candle they could pick up at the store. Unless there’s a fun theme that you’re certain appeals to the group attending, skip bringing a single candle to a white elephant exchange. Or make the candle part of a gift basket; our favorite tomato-scented candle goes great with some kitchen or garden accessories.
  • Puzzles. I think puzzles are hard to randomly gift—true puzzle fanatics will want a lot of pieces, while novices will want an easier one, and you never know which one you’ll get. If you choose a puzzle with too specific a theme, the receiver might not like it as much as a true puzzler or fan of that theme would, but it’s often not beloved enough to be steal-worthy.
  • Live animals. Look, you shouldn’t give baby chicks at Easter, and you shouldn’t give anything even remotely similar—including a mouse, fish, or anything alive.
  • Actual trash. I didn’t think I had to write this one down, but at one gift exchange I went to, someone literally wrapped up a piece of garbage as a joke. As the person who unwrapped the trash gift, I beg of you: Don’t do this.

Rules of a White Elephant

If you’re headed to your first white elephant gift exchange, here’s a quick explainer on what’s about to happen.

Everyone will bring a wrapped gift (often under a certain price, like $25) and place it into a pile or central spot. Then, each person will draw a number that indicates their place in the gift-choosing order. When your number is called, you can either choose and unwrap a gift from the pile, or steal one that has already been unwrapped by someone. Most exchanges will have a limit on how often a gift can be stolen—usually around three times—so if you have the best gift in your hands when it’s time for someone else to choose, there’s no guarantee you’ll get to keep it. If your gift is stolen, you can either unwrap a new one or steal someone else’s gift (no take-backs, sorry).

These rules can vary based on the host and their house rules, so make sure to ask what the rules are at the start of the game. Happy exchanging!

entries.title: Best Mesh Wi-Fi Systems (2026): I Tested Them All
entries.summary: Forget about patchy internet connections and dead spots in the house. These WIRED-tested, multi-room mesh Wi-Fi systems will keep your whole house online.
entries.content:
Routers are rarely placed in an ideal spot. Whether they're tucked into a closet or stuffed under your bed, the location is likely less-than-optimal for spreading reliable and fast internet across your entire house. Mesh routers promise to extend Wi-Fi coverage by enabling you to place a second or third node wherever you need, and they appear as a unified Wi-Fi network. Your devices will automatically connect to the nearest option for the best speeds.

Whether you want to fix dead zones, stop the buffering in the back bedroom, or get decent Wi-Fi in the backyard, a mesh Wi-Fi system could be the answer. The Netgear Orbi 770 Series is the best mesh Wi-Fi system for most people, but I have many alternatives to suit different homes and internet connections.

  • Best Mesh: Netgear Orbi 770 Series (3-Pack)
  • Best Subscription-Free Mesh: Asus ZenWiFi BT10 (2-Pack)
  • Upgrade Pick: Asus ZenWifi BQ16 Pro (2-Pack)
  • Best for Simplicity: Amazon Eero Pro 7 (3-Pack)
  • Best Budget: TP-Link Deco BE63 (3-Pack)
  • Best Wi-Fi 6 Mesh: Asus ZenWiFi XT8 (2-Pack)
  • Best Outdoor Mesh: TP-Link Deco BE25 Outdoor (1-Pack)

Note: The FCC's foreign-made router ban announced in March may stop any company that doesn't secure an exemption (Conditional Approval) from selling new mesh systems in the US, however, existing systems can continue to be sold (everything listed here). They can also be updated with new firmware, at least until January 1, 2029. So far, Netgear, Eero, and Asus, among others (here's the full list), have secured a Conditional Approval.

Before you dive deeper into my lineup, it’s a good idea to consider whether a mesh system is right for you. My guide on how to choose a router will help you answer that question and determine the features you need. If you don't want to switch to a new Wi-Fi mesh system, I also have advice on upgrading your existing Wi-Fi, the best Wi-Fi extenders, the best routers overall, and ways to secure and protect your home network.

Updated September 2026: I added more news about FCC Conditional Approvals for Asus and other manufacturers. I also updated my Asus picks with the NordVPN subscription offer, refreshed the FAQ with recent events, and added a section on access points.

Best Mesh Router System

If you're excited to upgrade to the latest Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, the Netgear Orbi 770 Series may be the best way to do so. This is the perfect mesh for the average family home. The Orbi 770 is backward compatible with older devices, but you need some Wi-Fi 7 devices, like an iPhone 17, Pixel 11 Pro, or M5 MacBook Air, to take full advantage of the benefits.

These towering routers aren’t quite as big as the far more expensive Orbi 970 Series, but they have a similar design and are still relatively large compared to most other mesh systems, like the Asus BT10 or Eero Pro 7 below. The main router has four 2.5 Gbps Ethernet ports, while the satellites make do with two 2.5 Gbps ports apiece. There’s no USB. Setup is quick and easy using the Orbi app on your phone.

It is a tri-band system, and by default, there is one network name (SSID) for the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands, and it supports multi-link operation (MLO). MLO is a new Wi-Fi 7 feature that allows devices to connect on multiple bands simultaneously. While a single SSID simplifies things, MLO can cause problems for legacy devices because Wi-Fi 7 has more stringent security requirements (WPA2 or higher). Something like an iPhone 5 won’t be able to connect, though you could potentially use a guest or IoT network.

Wi-Fi 7 also enables wider channels (up to 320 MHz from the current high of 160 MHz) and a handful of other improvements. You can expect consistently fast Wi-Fi and excellent coverage from this system (Netgear optimistically suggests up to 8,000 square feet for a three-pack). I found it fast and stable, and it had no issues covering my home. While it is slower than some other systems I tested, you are unlikely to notice the difference in everyday use unless you are constantly transferring large files.

The Orbi 770 offers more than enough bandwidth for multiple people in the household to be streaming and gaming simultaneously. There's potential for stable, low-latency, multi-gigabit speeds if you have Wi-Fi 7 devices connected to the main router, but I occasionally encountered a touch of lag with the satellites. If you can run Ethernet cables for wired backhaul, you can eliminate that.

The Orbi app is straightforward and shows connected clients, enabling you to check your internet speed and tweak a few other settings. You get 30-day trials of Netgear’s Smart Parental Controls and Armor security software (powered by Bitdefender), which gets you phishing and malware protection, as well as device and network scanning. After the trial is up, it costs $40 for the first year, then jumps to $100, while the parental controls (profiles, age-appropriate filters, scheduling, and time limits) are $8 per month. You don't need either of these pricey subscriptions.

Unless you have a very large home and a multi-gig internet connection (over 2.5 Gbps), this mesh is likely to be indistinguishable from more expensive mesh systems, like the TP-Link Deco BE85 ($1,200), Eero Max 7 ($1,700), and Netgear Orbi 970 Series ($2,000). In my previous modern home, I rarely noticed the enhanced performance of the much pricier 970 over the 770, and a two-pack will more than suffice for most folks. If your internet connection is faster than 2.5 Gbps, consider the excellent Netgear Orbi 870 (3-Pack) at $1,300. Watch out for frequent discounts on all of these systems.

Specs
Wi-Fi version Wi-Fi 7
Bands 6 GHz, 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz
Ports One 2.5 Gbps WAN, three 2.5 Gbps LAN (main), two 2.5 Gbps LAN (satellites)
Size 5.28 x 9.88 x 3.95 inches

Best Subscription-Free Mesh Router

This Wi-Fi 7 mesh system delivers strong coverage and impressive throughput. It is also a tri-band system (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz ) that uses MLO for a reliable wireless backhaul between the main router and mesh node. While I originally tested a two-pack in a modern, 1,600-square-foot home, the BT10 recently proved powerful enough for my challenging old Victorian house, which features thick stone walls and dampening rubble between the floors. Each unit also includes two 10-Gbps Ethernet ports, one Gigabit port, and a USB 3.0 port.

The BT10 is highly versatile—a hallmark of Asus systems—and can be configured via the mobile app or the web interface. Asus continues to offer comprehensive security software and parental controls at no extra cost, making this a great choice if you want to avoid monthly subscriptions. Competitors like Netgear, TP-Link, and Eero all charge for these extras. Just be aware that using AiProtection Pro means sharing data with Trend Micro, so you may want to review their privacy policy first. Once set up, the parental controls allow you to easily create profiles, schedule bedtimes, filter content by age, and review online activity.

Asus also has a partnership with NordVPN that gives you 1 year of NordVPN Standard with your purchase of this system and several others, including the BQ16 Pro and BT8 listed below (some cheaper systems get 6 months). You must upload a photo of your invoice and register your serial number to get a coupon code.

The BT10 is a feature-rich system. The Quality of Service option makes it easy to prioritize activities like working from home, gaming, or streaming, and you can limit bandwidth for specific devices. The BT10 also supports VPN services and 4G or 5G tethering. Asus gives you more access to tinker than most manufacturers. I appreciate having access to a wealth of settings, but you should be prepared to do a little tweaking and troubleshooting.

When I initially tested the BT10, I was hesitant to recommend it due to buggy firmware and overall system instability. I had trouble with my Sonos speakers disappearing (this may be the fault of Sonos), and my Pixel 9 dropping connection repeatedly, requiring a reset. But I’m pleased to report that the latest firmware seems to have stabilized things, and the BT10 has come down in price. I used it over the busy holiday period, and it was rock solid, offering impressive speed and range, excellent node performance for a wireless backhaul, and silky smooth transfer speeds on my home network, where I recently set up a NAS server. An issue I had with one PC was resolved by binding it to the main router. It hasn’t been flawless (my Pixel 10 Pro XL still sometimes dropped connection when handing off between nodes, though it generally righted itself within a few seconds).

While I had a much better experience the second time around—with the BT10 comfortably outperforming the Deco BE67 it replaced in my home—mixed online reviews suggest your mileage may vary. Still, the potential reward is top-notch, subscription-free networking. If you want most of these benefits in a slightly slower but significantly cheaper package, the Asus BT8 (listed below) is a great alternative.

Specs
Wi-Fi Version Wi-Fi 7
Bands 6 GHz, 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz
Ports One 10 Gbps WAN/LAN, one 10 Gbps LAN, and one Gigabit WAN/LAN, one USB 3.0
Size 6.25 x 7.32 x 2.83 inches

Upgrade Pick

Topping my charts in almost every test, this is the fastest mesh system I have reviewed. It delivers speedy, stable Wi-Fi across an impressively wide area using a quad-band setup—adding a second 6-GHz band to the usual 2.4-, 5-, and 6-GHz bands. Packed with versatile features, it takes full advantage of everything Wi-Fi 7 has to offer.

I tested a two-pack of the BQ16 Pro, which looks similar to the BT10 but is slightly larger to accommodate the internal antennas needed for its expansive coverage (Asus claims up to 8,000 square feet). This system handled my thick-walled old home admirably, delivering a far stronger signal to the furthest rooms than any other system I’ve tested. I even managed to get a reliable connection in my garage, which is usually a complete dead spot.

Setup was a breeze using the Asus Router app on my phone, though it’s best to keep the node close until it’s up and running. Each unit has two 10-Gbps Ethernet ports, three Gigabit ports, and a USB 3.0 port. It’s perfect for a multi-gig internet connection, and you could run wired backhaul to maximize speeds throughout your home.

Like the BT10, everything you could want is included here, from free parental controls and security software to VPN support (including a free year of NordVPN) and Quality of Service options to prioritize specific activities or devices. This mesh is a dream for power users who love delving into settings and playing around. Because it was originally released in 2024, the BQ16 Pro has benefited from several firmware updates and is now rock-solid. I experienced no early bugs, and no new issues have emerged over the past three months of testing. This is the system I consistently return to after testing others.

As great as it is, the BQ16 Pro is overkill for most folks. The BT10 is almost as good and will likely serve just fine in most homes. But if you have a large house or thick walls and dampening, like I do, you will notice the upgrade. Provided you don’t mind spending the cash, this is an excellent, feature-packed mesh system that can do it all.

Specs
Wi-Fi Version Wi-Fi 7
Bands 2x 6 GHz, 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz
Ports One 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, one 10-Gbps LAN, one Gigabit WAN/LAN, two Gigabit LANs, one USB 3.0
Size 6.9 x 8.6 x 2.8 inches

Best for Simplicity

Amazon’s Eero mesh systems are the easiest to set up, offer fairly wide coverage, and deliver stable connectivity. The Eero Pro 7 is an elegant system, available as two or three identical routers. Eero switched to a tower design to enable a better antenna array for wider coverage, but the Pro 7 units still blend in easily on a table or shelf. Each one has a USB-C port for power and two Ethernet ports rated at 5 Gbps. Designed as a hands-off, set-and-forget system, it fully supports Wi-Fi 7 across the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands.

The Eero Pro 7 is a strong performer, delivering impressively low lag and stable bandwidth sharing across many devices, with zero drops during my testing. The mobile app is straightforward, allowing you to easily view connected devices, pause the internet, and set up a guest network. You can also create profiles to group devices and set schedules. Unfortunately, unlocking content filtering, advanced security, ad blocking, and deeper activity insights requires a costly Eero Plus subscription ($10 per month or $100 per year).

Eero is an Amazon company, and its routers come with Alexa support. Enable the Eero skill, and you can pause the internet with a voice command through your Echo device, which is handy when your child won’t get off the computer to eat dinner. The Eero Pro 7 also supports Matter and Thread, and it can double as a Zigbee smart home hub just like an Echo device. This allows you to directly connect compatible smart lighting, locks, and other accessories, making it a great choice if you have a lot of smart home gear.

Two other tricks make an Eero mesh network attractive. An Echo (4th Gen), Echo Dot (4th or 5th Gen), or Echo Dot with clock (4th or 5th Gen) smart speaker can act as a Wi-Fi extender, offering an extra 1,000 square feet of coverage at speeds up to 100 Mbps for up to 10 devices. Eero also offers an Internet Backup option, so you can add multiple backup networks (Wi-Fi or hotspot) to keep you online if your main wired network goes down.

Eero’s simplicity will appeal to anyone who hates digging into settings, but there’s a cost. You won’t find any Quality of Service features for prioritizing traffic, and you can’t separate Wi-Fi bands. And while the two Ethernet ports allow for a wired backhaul, using them leaves no room to plug in other wired devices. While basic Eero systems sometimes suffer from slow transfer speeds, that wasn't an issue with the Pro 7. It offers slick and smooth tri-band Wi-Fi 7 at a reasonable price, making it the sweet spot in Eero's current lineup.

A few Eero systems on the market are worth considering, delivering a broadly similar experience. The first two are dual-band systems (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz). Although the basic Eero 6 ($270) was one of the slower systems I tested, particularly at longer distances, it is likely perfectly fine for modest needs and internet plans up to 500 Mbps. If you have a faster connection, up to 1 Gbps, and a home smaller than 4,500 square feet, then the Eero 6+ ($300) is a great step up.

If you want a Wi-Fi 7 system for a smaller home, consider the Eero 7 ($400). While it is only a dual-band system—meaning you'll miss out on the faster 6-GHz band—you still get other Wi-Fi 7 advantages like including MLO and enhanced security. It performed respectably in my tests with solid speeds, but its limited range means it won't be a good fit for everyone. Mesh Wi-Fi Systems: Your Questions, Answered

What Is a Mesh Wi-Fi System?

A mesh Wi-Fi system consists of a main router that connects to your modem and one or more satellite nodes placed throughout your home. The entire system broadcasts a single network name (SSID) and password, automatically handing your devices off to whichever node provides the strongest signal as you move from room to room. It's a fantastic choice for those who have multiple stories in their home that they need to reliably cover.

What Should I Consider When Shopping for a Mesh System?

Here are a few points to keep in mind when you are buying a new mesh Wi-Fi system.

Wi-Fi standards: Many devices support Wi-Fi 7 now. Many of the best laptops and phones do, and it’s only growing more common (the iPhone 16 and iPhone 17 range support it). All the models I recommend as main picks support at least Wi-Fi 6, and they are backward compatible with older Wi-Fi standards. If you have a lot of new devices, consider Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7. While the first Wi-Fi 8 mesh systems will land later this year, the official certification is still a couple of years away. Our router shopping guide goes into more depth.

Internet speeds: There are many ways to upgrade your Wi-Fi, but your internet speed is limited by your internet service provider (ISP). If the maximum speed of data coming to your modem is 100 Mbps, that’s the fastest possible connection that any router can provide.

Bands: The top speed that router manufacturers claim on the box is all of the bands added together, which is disingenuous since you usually only connect to one band at a time. MLO is a feature in Wi-Fi 7 that enables you connect on multiple bands simultaneously but you will still never achieve the top speeds that manufacturers state.

Coverage: While it’s good to have an idea of a router’s coverage and speed, understand that your mileage may vary. The construction materials in your house, your neighbors’ proximity and Wi-Fi networks, the devices you have with wireless connectivity, and the position of routers and nodes in your home are just some of the factors that can impact the performance of your Wi-Fi.

Backhaul: Backhaul channels are reserved for one mesh router or node to talk to another. It’s common for mesh routers to have a dedicated backhaul channel, enabling the main router to provide speeds as close to your full internet speed as possible to any node. This is also important for local network speed and may impact the performance of network-attached storage (NAS) systems, remote console play, and how quickly you can copy a file from one wireless device on your network to another.

QoS: Quality of Service allows you to prioritize the Wi-Fi connection for specific activities and their related apps or for specific devices. You can use it to ensure gaming, streaming, or video calls take precedence, which can be very handy in any household with limited bandwidth.

Ports: Ports and cables can help establish more stable connections. They may be essential if you have smart home hubs for lights and security cameras or network-attached storage that needs to plug into your main router. But they can also be useful on nodes to plug in streaming devices or game consoles and get the full benefit of any dedicated backhaul channel speeds your chosen system might offer.

Mesh vs. router: Although mesh systems are tempting, many homes will be better served by a single, well-placed Wi-Fi router. Check out the Best Wi-Fi Routers for options. Some of the routers I tested in the modern two-floor 1,600-square-foot home I used to live in performed just as well or better than mesh systems, but the old Victorian house I live in now, although not much bigger, has very thick walls and really needs a mesh.

Security: Most routers come with optional subscriptions for security, parental controls, and sometimes other extras like VPN service. You don't need these subscriptions, but they can be handy and provide peace of mind. Just make sure you factor in the cost or opt for a system from a manufacturer like Asus, which offers them for free.

Wait for sales: Mesh systems tend to be very expensive when first released and are often buggy. By waiting a few months, you can expect deep discounts (50 percent is not unusual) and firmware updates that ensure more stable performance.

What Are the Benefits of a Mesh System?

Easy setup is part of the appeal of mesh Wi-Fi systems, and they generally have a companion app that should guide you through the process. Mesh systems are designed to automatically manage your network, deciding on the correct bands and Wi-Fi channels for different devices to ensure a speedy and stable connection.

Mobile apps generally make it easy to check on connected devices and tweak basic settings when needed. They often offer parental controls, network security, guest network, and device or activity prioritization features, but sometimes these require a paid subscription. Mesh systems are also expandable, so you can add more nodes should you need to. Many mesh manufacturers, such as Eero, enable you to mix and match mesh systems from different ranges.

What Are the Disadvantages of a Mesh System?

The main downside to mesh systems is price, as they're generally more expensive than single routers. You may find speeds from nodes are significantly reduced compared to the main router if you rely on wireless backhaul. Mesh systems are not suitable for every home and can often be outperformed by a good, well-placed single router. Each node also requires a good spot within range of the main router with an outlet. I break this down further in mesh system vs. Wi-Fi router.

Is Mesh Router Location Important?

Poor placement of nodes is the main mistake people make with a mesh system. Nodes must be within range of the main router and need a strong signal. Think of a mesh system as the Wi-Fi backbone of your home, and avoid placing nodes at the extremities. It’s also crucial not to place nodes next to potential obstructions (metal, furniture, mirrors) or hide them away in cabinets. You also may want to avoid potential interference from other electronics like microwaves, baby monitors, and TVs. While people often place nodes too far away from the main router, placing them too close together can also reduce their effectiveness. Ideally, nodes should be anywhere between 30 and 50 feet from the router, or no more than two rooms away.

Are Mesh Systems Better Than Wi-Fi Extenders?

Mesh systems are superior to even the best Wi-Fi extenders for most folks seeking whole home coverage. Wi-Fi extenders take the Wi-Fi signal from your router and use the same frequency band to repeat the signal. You can expect slower speeds (50 percent of your main router speed is the maximum, but it’s usually much lower), higher latency, and smart home issues. They also tend to plug directly into outlets, making it tough to position them well. Cheap extenders don’t work well, and good ones are so expensive that you are better served by upgrading your router or buying a mesh system. The one case where it may be worth buying an extender is when you have a single trouble spot in your home.

Should I Choose a Wi-Fi 6 or a Wi-Fi 7 Mesh?

While Wi-Fi 6 is enough for most homes for now, Wi-Fi 7 brings improvements in bandwidth and speed, among other things, though you can expect coverage to be similar. Most Wi-Fi 7 mesh systems are still more expensive. There are some cheaper dual-band Wi-Fi 7 systems, but they miss out on the 6-GHz band, simply offering the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands we are used to. Unless you are connecting your mesh routers with Ethernet cables to create a wired backhaul, a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 system will likely perform worse than a similarly priced tri-band Wi-Fi 6 mesh (with two 5-GHz bands and one 2.4 GHz) in most homes, because it has to use the available bands for wireless backhaul (traffic between the router and nodes). If you want to try the 6-GHz band, Wi-Fi 6E mesh systems offer a more affordable way to do so.

All that said, if you have a very busy household with a lot of devices or want something that'll last for a few years and don’t mind paying for it, a tri- or quad-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh is the way to go. If you currently have issues with latency or bandwidth, or you simply want the latest features, such as MLO enabling devices to connect on multiple bands, Wi-Fi 7 is worthwhile.

Is Wired or Wireless Backhaul Better?

As I explained above, backhaul channels allow your main router to send traffic back and forth to your nodes. For the best stability, security, and speed, you should definitely run Ethernet cables between your router and mesh nodes. Many folks can't or don't want to run cables, and mesh systems can establish a wireless backhaul for this reason.

If you can't run cables, it's worth considering a mesh system that has a dedicated band for wireless backhaul, or perhaps a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 system capable of using MLO for wireless backhaul, for best performance. I recommend avoiding dual-band mesh systems if you plan to go with wireless backhaul, because they'll have to use the same single 5-GHz band for node and connected device traffic.

Can I Add Mesh Wi-Fi to an Existing Router?

You can add a mesh system to your existing standalone router, but it’s not always the best idea. Ideally, you will have a separate modem that you can plug your mesh directly into, and you can remove your old router. If you have a combined router and modem supplied by your Internet Service Provider (ISP), you may need to plug your mesh system into that, but you should set your ISP’s router into bridge mode. Ensure you check compatibility, as some mesh systems have limitations when used this way.

Some manufacturers also offer single routers that have mesh support, so you can add mesh systems or additional routers to create a mesh. These are usually proprietary, such as AiMesh from Asus, so you can only mix routers from that manufacturer. There is an open standard called EasyMesh, but only TP-Link offers wide support across its range. If you decide to mix and match, it’s best to pick devices that support the same Wi-Fi standard with broadly similar specs.

What About the US Ban on Foreign-Made Routers?

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US because of national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market must be approved.

The way the ban is described, it applies to every new mesh system, because there are currently no companies manufacturing routers or the components they are assembled from in the US. But companies can apply for exemptions.

All new models of foreign-produced routers will require Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security before the FCC can clear them for sale in the US. Read Everything You Need to Know About the Foreign-Made Router Ban in the US to learn more.

What About Firmware and Security Updates?

While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.”

What happens after that date is not clear, but if the FCC were to block further updates for the routers and mesh systems folks already own, it would exacerbate the very issue it is trying to address. The majority of routers that are compromised and used in cyberattacks are usually older devices that no longer receive security updates.

Should I Buy a Mesh Router Now?

If you live in the US and need a router or a mesh, you should buy one. Asus, Netgear, Eero, and a few others have been granted Conditional Approval already. All the other major manufacturers I asked who responded or have released a statement, including TP-Link and Synology, are confident about getting exemptions, though whether they will is impossible to say for sure. An FCC spokesperson told me, “We expect approvals to be granted in a timely manner.”

The problem with waiting is that prices are likely to go up. I've already seen some price creep on systems from TP-Link, Netgear, and Eero, though this could also be due to the AI-driven RAM shortage.

How I Test Mesh Routers

To test the best Wi-Fi mesh systems, I use each one for at least a week (usually longer) in a busy family home of four with lots of video streaming, gaming, and video calls. I also test the mobile apps and web interfaces to see how easy it is to change settings, set up parental controls, and access security features. My priority is to learn how well the mesh works in real-life rather than a lab, but I do also run a set of standardized tests, so that I have numbers to compare.

I run speed tests (downloads and uploads). I transfer files on the network on multiple devices (including iPhones, Android phones, Windows PCs, and MacBooks) from different spots around my home, including files from devices connected to the main router to devices connected to nodes. I use NetSpot to survey signal strength throughout the house and create heat maps for comparison. I run the TamoSoft Throughput Test, and I turn the power and modem off and on to find out how each system recovers.

How I Select Mesh Routers to be Reviewed

I try to test as many mesh releases as possible and have put more than 40 systems through their paces. (A handful of those have since been discontinued, but most are reviewed on this page.) It’s not possible to test every device, so while I will typically test flagship systems, I also strive to find more affordable systems and identify models that will suit the average family home in terms of budget and performance.

We are brand agnostic, so we will test systems from any manufacturer, provided we can get ahold of them. The manufacturers or their PR companies provide all the mesh systems we test. We do lean toward testing more systems from the most popular brands. I would love to test one of Ubiquiti’s mesh systems but have been unable to secure one so far.

Most products are loaned for a month or so and then returned. A handful of our recommended picks are kept for longer-term testing. The remainder are donated to charities. I recently dropped off a batch to Reusing IT and have donated several devices to Oxfam and Shelter.
